sections.heading: Dialogue I, Knot viii, part 2 (printed pp. 65–69)
rows: [p. 65] Andab. {?Ohe}, manum de tabula, Ereuni; monet Aristoteles pauca esse quae de coelis nosci possunt, accidentia eorum pauca ad nos deferri. Et (quod nos propius spectat) tot saeculis inauditum quicquam apud superos innovatum esse.

[p. 65] Andab. Ho there [Ohe], hand off the picture [manum de tabula], Ereunius; Aristotle warns that few are the things which can be known about the heavens, [that] few of their accidents are carried down to us. And (what regards us more nearly) [that] in so many ages [it is] unheard of that anything has been innovated among those above [apud superos].

Deinde non hoc saltem vides? si ex nostris elementis compacta forent illa corpora communem saltem nostratium legem subitura, ut sponte sua centro se appli- [p. 66] carent? quod vides non nisi cum universi ruina contingere posse.

Then do you not see this at least? if those bodies were compacted out of our elements, [they would be] about to undergo [subitura] at least the common law of our [bodies] [nostratium], that of their own accord they should appl- [p. 66] y themselves to the centre? which you see cannot happen except with the ruin of the universe.
Ereu. Tempori suggessisti quae oportuit: At ego tibi experimenta neque levia, neque pauca promitto, si prius quaenam expectanda putes, exposueris.

Ereu. You have suggested in good time [tempori] what was fitting: but I promise you experiments [experimenta] neither light nor few, if you shall first have set out which [ones] you think are to be expected.
Fortassis enim quae apud nos vides hortorum et agrorum culturam, et succedentes pro anni vicissitudine telluris vel aquarum foetus depromi tibi ex penu flagitas. Haec fateor non posse praestare.

For perhaps you demand that the things which you see among us, the culture of gardens and of fields, and the offspring [foetus] of the earth [telluris] or of the waters succeeding according to the vicissitude of the year, be brought out for you from the store-cupboard [penu]. These, I confess, [I] cannot furnish [praestare].
Si vero e tam longinquis plagis non nisi ingentes quasdam mutationes petis, vide quam rarae sint apud nos hae novitates. Quae idcirco praemitto ut qua frequentia contentus esse debeas, intelligas.

But if from regions so far off you seek nothing but certain enormous mutations, see how rare among us are these novelties. Which [things] I send ahead [praemitto] for this reason, that you may understand with what frequency you ought to be content.
[Margin: Experimenta Corruptibilitatis in Sole.] Primum itaque e sole ostentum promo cuius nobis evaporationem vel candido sermone fumos ostendit Galilaeus.

[Margin: Experiments of Corruptibility in the Sun.] First, therefore, I bring forth from the sun a portent [ostentum], whose evaporation, or in candid speech [candido sermone] fumes [fumos], Galileo shows to us.

Unde duo manifeste concluduntur et Solem paulatim deteri (nisi aliunde alimentum sumat) et proprium nostrique similem in coelis ignem esse; quamquam lumen non aliud quam flammam puram esse in eo quem citavi libello, extra aleam positum existimem.

Whence two [things] are manifestly concluded: both that the Sun is little by little rubbed away (unless it takes nourishment from elsewhere), and that there is in the heavens a fire proper [proprium] and like ours; although [that] light is nothing other than pure flame, I should judge [existimem] [to have been] placed beyond the die [extra aleam] in that little book which I cited.
Neque ego pro Aristotele fidem pacisci piger sim, eum, si ignem in coelestibus deprehendisset, caetera quoque elementa de sublimi suspensurum fuisse.

Nor would I be slow to stake [pacisci] [my] pledge [fidem] on behalf of Aristotle, that he, if he had detected fire in the celestial [things], would have hung the other elements also from on high [de sublimi].

Agnatum est huic experimento aliud, in eodem solo particulas alias aliis esse fulgidiores et lucis magis vividae. Non vides escam [p. 67] flammis solaribus subiectam et fontes quosdam lucis seu flammae ad exteriora, ut ita dicam evomitae.

Born-alongside [agnatum] this experiment is another: that in the same ground [solo] some particles are more resplendent than others and of more vivid light. Do you not see fuel [escam] [p. 67] laid under the solar flames, and certain fountains of light or flame vomited out, so to speak, to the outer [parts].

[Margin: Ex Luna & & stellis.] In Luna montes et valles alia lucidiora, alia opaciora. Crassum circiter aerem qui et Lunares montes aspectui nostro laeviget, et Solem in eclypsibus interdum circulo luminoso exundare faciat.

[Margin: From the Moon and and the stars.] In the Moon, mountains and valleys, some more lucid, others more opaque. A thick air round about, which both smooths [laeviget] the Lunar mountains to our view, and makes the Sun in eclipses sometimes overflow [exundare] with a luminous circle.

Adiice his stellas subventaneas. In Cassiopaea, in cycno et alibi iam familiare Astronomis phasma. Bone Deus! cuius altitudinis, cuius magnitudinis et fulgoris? at vitae brevis et mortis non subitariae, sed Phthisis spectabilis.

Add to these the wind-[begotten] stars [stellas subventaneas]. In Cassiopeia, in the swan [cycno] and elsewhere, a phantasm [phasma] already familiar to the Astronomers. Good God! of what height, of what magnitude and brightness? but of brief life, and of a death not sudden but of a visible Consumption [Phthisis spectabilis].

[Margin: Chaldaeorum impostura.] Ex quibus ni laevus sim, mendacii coarguntur Chaldaei, qui cum tot millia annorum sese venditent Astrorum metiendis viis impendisse et numeris collecta habuisse, nihil tamen nobis de tam insigni coelestium corporum nascitura prodiderunt.

[Margin: The imposture of the Chaldaeans.] From which [things], unless I am left-handed [laevus], the Chaldaeans are convicted of a lie, who, although they vaunt [venditent] themselves to have spent so many thousands of years on measuring the ways of the Stars, and to have had [them] collected in numbers, yet have handed down to us nothing about so notable a birth [nascitura] of celestial bodies.

Valeat itaque eos Graecis priores fuisse et in principiis magistros, sed tot volumina ad authoritatem conciliandam finxisse: praeterquam enim quod annos mundo antiquiores spondeant, quale est ut Graeci et eorum sectatores duobus annorum millibus suopte Marte Astronomiam ex ipsis incunabulis in hanc amplitudinem vocaverint, Illi post ingentem hiatum de perennitate et assiduitate et accuratissima observatione nihil ultra prima et rudia principia, in medium nobis contulerint?

Let it stand [valeat], therefore, that they were prior to the Greeks and masters in the beginnings [principiis], but that they feigned so many volumes for winning authority: for besides that they pledge years more ancient than the world, of what sort is it [quale est] that the Greeks and their followers in two thousand years by their own Mars [suopte Marte] should have called Astronomy from its very cradle into this amplitude, [and that] They, after an enormous gaping [hiatum] about perennity and assiduity and most accurate observation, should have brought into the middle [in medium] for us nothing beyond the first and rude principles [principia]?

Ultimum a Cometis testimonium flagito quos [p. 68] in Coelum iampridem sustulerunt Astronomi, cum non aliam quam fixa sydera patiantur aspectus varietatem; quos tamen ortum et mutationem et interitum sortiri vel oculis testibus agnoscimus.

The last testimony I demand from the Comets, which [p. 68] the Astronomers long since raised up into the Heaven, since they suffer no other variety of aspect [aspectus varietatem] than the fixed stars [suffer]; which nevertheless we acknowledge, even with the eyes as witnesses, to obtain [sortiri] rising [ortum] and mutation and destruction.
Habes testes extra aleam positos ex omni coelesti plaga in tuam curiam, Andabata, citatos, quos si contempseris ipsos adversarios advocabo, non Peripateticos sed Peripateticorum simios.

You have witnesses placed beyond the die [extra aleam], summoned from every celestial region into your court [curiam], Andabata; whom if you shall have despised, I shall call in [advocabo] the adversaries themselves, not Peripatetics but apes of the Peripatetics.

Si enim veri Aristotelis cultores essent, praecepta ipsius de praeferenda veritate, et monita de incertitudine quam in coelestibus secutus est, attenderent. Prudens enim lector ubi viderit in quam dissimiles veri sententias se abiiciant, non aliud illustrius vanitatis caelicae incorruptionis argumentum poterit desiderare.

For if they were true [veri] cultivators of Aristotle, they would attend to his precepts about truth being preferred, and [his] warnings about the uncertainty which he followed in celestial [things]. For a prudent reader, when he shall have seen into what opinions [sententias] unlike the true [veri] they throw themselves, will be able to desire no other more illustrious argument of the vanity of the heavenly [caelicae] incorruption.

Cum e diverso, quomodo potentissima est necessitas, si haec in Coelo mutentur, passibilia esse Astra et Coelos alterabiles: Sic posito tales esse Coelos et sidera, nihil infirmiori sequelarum catena trahitur, haec omnia suis existere debere periodis.

Since, from the opposite side [e diverso], just as the necessity is most powerful, if these things are changed in the Heaven, [that] the Stars are passible and the Heavens alterable: So, it being posited that the Heavens and stars are such, by a chain of consequences [sequelarum] in no way weaker is it drawn [that] all these things must exist in their periods.
Si enim Sol igneus est fumos necesse est egredi et circumagitari. Necesse item alias partes splendidiores, alias minus lucentes habere. Necesse est ex Luna vapores, sicut ex terra educere.

For if the Sun is fiery, it is necessary that fumes go out and be driven around. Necessary likewise [that it] have some parts more splendid, others less shining. It is necessary [for it] to draw out [educere] vapours from the Moon, as from the earth [terra].

Necesse est et in aliis Planetis similia contingere, et in superiori Coelo quo maiora sunt corpora, eo etiam insigniora apparere portenta. Esse exhalationum diffusiora ar- [p. 69] [Margin: Nodus IX. De Cometarum generatione et natura.] menta quae Stellarum et Cometarum species ad nos demittant, et (quoniam magna pleraque constantiora sunt) non exiguo sese spatio conservent. [Knot ix continues on p. 69 with 'Andab. Quid etiamne barbas Cometis'.]

It is necessary both that similar things happen in the other Planets, and that in the higher Heaven, by how much the bodies are greater, by so much more notable portents also appear. That there are more diffused he- [p. 69] [Margin: Knot IX. On the generation and nature of Comets.] rds [armenta] of exhalations, which send down to us the appearances [species] of Stars and Comets, and (since great things are for the most part more constant) preserve themselves for no small space. [Knot ix continues on p. 69 with 'Andab. Quid etiamne barbas Cometis'.]

terms: Interjection of satiety: 'enough!' (Plautus; Horace, Sat. II.5.96 'ohe iam!').
Proverb: 'stop working on it, enough'; from Apelles' fault of never knowing when to stop (Pliny NH 35.80; Cicero, Fam. VII.25).
Andabata tells Ereunius to stop elaborating.
Usually 'among the gods' or 'in the upper world'; here = in the heavens.
Aristotle, De caelo I.3 270b13–16: no change recorded in the outermost heaven in all past time.
'Our countrymen'; here bodies of our world.
Natural place: heavy bodies tend to the centre.
Domestic image: Ereunius cannot deliver gardens and crops from the heavens.
Prodigy, sign; here a striking appearance.
'candidus' = plain, frank, with a pun on the Sun's whiteness.
Galileo, Istoria e dimostrazioni intorno alle macchie solari (1613), compared sunspots to clouds or smoke.
Gambling metaphor; also used of the 'testes' below.
in that little book which I cited
Digby, Of Bodies, ch. 8: light is fire/flame in its rarest state.
Irony: Aristotle would have put all elements in the heavens.
Legal: related through the male line; also a later-born offshoot.
'solum' = ground, base, surface; perhaps a misprint for 'sole' (sun).
Faculae: bright patches on the Sun (Scheiner, Galileo).
The sun's matter as fuel to its flames.
Kepler's view; the solar corona in eclipses attributed to a lunar atmosphere.
From 'ova subventanea' (wind-eggs, Pliny NH 10.166): empty, unfertile, spurious.
The novae of 1572 (Cassiopeia, Tycho) and 1600 (P Cygni).
Technical in Aristotle Meteor. I.5 for celestial apparitions.
The novae faded gradually rather than vanishing suddenly.
'laevus' = left, clumsy, foolish; also unlucky/lucky in augury.
Rare noun (Pliny) = birth, not the future participle.
Could also be 'farewell to [the claim]'; read as concessive 'granted'.
Proverbial: by their own unaided strength.
Open mouth, boasting; also a gap.
Mocks the Chaldaean claims (Cicero, Div. II.97: 470,000 years).
= contribute to the common stock, publish.
Tycho (De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis, 1588): comet of 1577 had no sensible parallax, so supralunar.
Legal metaphor of witnesses and advocates.
White distinguishes Aristotle from the schoolmen.
'veri' could grammatically be 'of the true Aristotle'; nominative plural agreeing with cultores is preferred.
Herds of cattle; perhaps a metaphor for drifting masses.
Possibly suggested by the 'barbae'/'comae' image; cf. Aristotle's dry exhalation as the matter of comets (Meteor. I.7).
notes: Unit: Dialogue I, Knot viii, part 2 of 2. PDF pp. 76–80 = printed pp. 65–69, from Andabata's '{?Ohe}, manum de tabula' (p. 65) to Ereunius' '…non exiguo sese spatio conservent.' (p. 69). Offset +11 holds (p. 69 = PDF 80).

Knot boundary: the margin 'Nodus IX. De Cometarum generatione & natura.' is printed at the top of p. 69 beside the last five lines of Ereunius' speech (whose closing sentence, begun on p. 68, already turns to comets). Andabata's question 'Quid etiamne barbas Cometis…' on p. 69 opens the comet discussion, so Knot ix is taken to start there; the end of Ereunius' speech is kept whole in this part and the margin is placed where printed.

Readings: (a) p. 65 printed 'Che' read as {?Ohe}. (b) p. 67 margin printed 'Ex Lunâ & & stellis' (dittography kept). (c) p. 66 'in eodem solo' kept as printed; 'sole' may be intended. (d) p. 66 'elcam' = escam (long s). (e) p. 67 'Non vides … evomitae.' is printed with a full stop, rendered as a question. (f) 'caelicae' (p. 68) spelled with ae, as printed. No illegible words.

Verification pass: the Latin was re-checked against 150 dpi pages and 300 dpi zooms (p. 65 'Che', p. 66 margin, p. 67 margins, p. 68 'caelicae'), and the English was checked against the Latin sentence by sentence. 6 corrections: (1) 'praestare' is active, '[I] cannot furnish', not passive; (2) 'veri' taken with 'cultores' ('true cultivators'), not 'of the true Aristotle'; (3) 'viderit' and 'contempseris' given future-perfect force; (4) 'educere' given the Sun as subject ('[for it] to draw out'), not passive; (5) 'vocaverint … contulerint' rendered as subjunctives in the 'quale est ut' clause; (6) 'exposueris' future perfect ('shall have set out').
Conventions as in glossary.md. Spellings kept: coelum/caelicus, sydera, eclypsibus, authoritatem, Cassiopaea, cycno, expectanda.
